blocks.prompt: The Horn That Is Not a Horn
blocks.text: Reach up and touch your fingernail. Now think about a rhino's horn. They are made of the same thing. It is called keratin, and it is the stuff in your nails and your hair. A rhino's horn has no bone inside it at all. It is packed keratin, pressed together hard, growing up out of the skin on the nose. Because it grows like a fingernail, it never stops growing. A rhino wears its horn down by rubbing it on rocks and by pushing at the ground. It uses the horn to dig for water in a dry riverbed, to snap branches, and to steer its calf along the path. There are five kinds of rhino left in the world. Two live in Africa and three live in Asia. Some have two horns and some have one. All of them are in trouble, because people hunt them for those horns, which are worth nothing more than a handful of fingernails.

blocks.prompt: Two Lips, Two Lives
blocks.text: Africa has two kinds of rhino, and the fastest way to tell them apart is to look at the mouth. The white rhino has a wide, flat upper lip, shaped almost like the front of a lawn mower. It walks with its head low, sweeping that broad lip across the ground, cropping short grass. It is a grazer. It is also enormous: a big male can weigh more than two tons, which makes it the largest land animal on Earth after the elephant. The black rhino has a completely different mouth. Its upper lip comes to a point and can grip like a finger. It uses that lip to pull leaves and twigs off thorny bushes, folding them into its mouth. It is a browser, and it carries its head high to reach the branches. The two names are confusing, because neither animal is white and neither is black. Both are gray. The names tell you nothing. The lips tell you everything. Neither rhino sees well. A rhino can barely make out a person standing thirty feet away. What it has instead is a nose that reads the wind and ears that swivel like dishes, tracking a sound without the head ever turning. The differences run deeper than food. White rhinos are the sociable ones and will gather in small groups. Black rhinos usually keep to themselves and have a reputation for charging first and looking later. Even their calves behave differently. A white rhino calf trots along in front of its mother, where she can watch it. A black rhino calf follows behind her, in the tunnel her body makes through the brush.

blocks.prompt: Fifty Rhinos, and What Came After
blocks.text: In the late 1800s, the southern white rhino was declared gone. Hunters had worked their way across southern Africa with such thoroughness that naturalists closed the file and moved on. Then, in 1895, a small population was found surviving in a valley in what is now KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. Estimates of how many were left vary, but every estimate is small: somewhere between fifty and a hundred animals. Every southern white rhino alive today descends from that one group. What happened next is the largest conservation success story of its kind. The valley was protected. The animals were counted, guarded, and eventually moved, a few at a time, to other reserves where rhinos had once lived and no longer did. The population climbed past a thousand, then past ten thousand. Today there are more than fifteen thousand southern white rhinos. A species that had been written off filled an entire continent's worth of parks again, and it did it in a century. That is the good half. The other half arrived with money. A rhino horn is keratin, chemically the same material as a fingernail, and it has no medicinal power whatsoever. This has been tested and retested. It does not matter. Because some buyers believe otherwise, horn has been priced by weight alongside gold, and poaching has surged. South Africa alone has lost hundreds of rhinos a year for over a decade. Meanwhile the northern white rhino, a separate population from farther up the continent, ran out of time. Two females remain. Both live under armed guard in Kenya, and neither can carry a calf. Scientists are attempting to rescue the population with stored cells and surrogate mothers. Whether that counts as saving a species is a question worth arguing about. Rangers have responded to the poaching with a strange, sad tactic: they find rhinos, sedate them, and cut off their horns. The horn is keratin, so cutting it hurts no more than a haircut, and it grows back within a few years. A dehorned rhino is a less valuable target. It is also a rhino that cannot dig properly for water, cannot defend its calf as well, and does not look like a rhino. Conservationists argue about it constantly. The argument is not really about horns. It is about how much of an animal you are willing to take away in order to keep it alive.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Order Perissodactyla: odd-toed, like horses and tapirs
Paraceratherium: a hornless rhino relative, nearly sixteen feet at the shoulder
Coelodonta, the woolly rhino, walked the Ice Age steppe
Keratin does not fossilize, so ancient horns are inferred from the skull
Rhinos vanished from North America about four million years ago
Five species are left, three of them critically endangered

blocks.prompt: A Family Down to Five
blocks.text: Start with the thing everyone knows and get it out of the way. A rhinoceros horn is not a horn. Cattle horns and antelope horns are built around a core of living bone. A rhino's is not. It is a solid mass of keratin, the identical protein in a fingernail, a hoof, and a strand of hair, compressed into a spike and anchored to a roughened patch of the skull rather than growing out of it. Cut it and it grows back. This is a fact with consequences, and we will come back to it. Now widen the frame. The rhinoceros belongs to an order called Perissodactyla, the odd-toed ungulates, animals that carry their weight down the middle toe. Its living relatives are not the elephant or the hippopotamus, which are unrelated heavyweights, but the horse and the tapir. There are fewer than twenty species of odd-toed ungulate left on Earth. That number should stop you. Thirty million years ago this was one of the dominant orders of large land mammals, and rhinos were its most successful branch. They were everywhere, and they were not what you are picturing. Paraceratherium, a hornless rhino relative that browsed the tops of trees in Asia, stood nearly sixteen feet at the shoulder and is one of the largest land mammals that has ever lived. Teleoceras was squat and barrel-bodied and lived in North American rivers like a hippo; hundreds of them lie preserved in a Nebraska waterhole, suffocated by ash that drifted a thousand miles from an eruption in Idaho twelve million years ago. Coelodonta, the woolly rhino, walked the Ice Age steppe alongside mammoths, and Stone Age painters put it on cave walls in France. Elasmotherium, the so-called Siberian unicorn, carried what was probably an enormous single horn and survived to within about thirty-nine thousand years ago, which means people almost certainly saw one. Notice the word probably. We have never found that horn. Keratin rots; it does not fossilize the way bone does. Everything we claim about a fossil rhino's horn is inferred from the rough, pitted patch of skull where the horn was cemented. The horn is the one part of a rhinoceros that time refuses to keep. Five species remain. Two in Africa, three in Asia. The Sumatran rhino, reddish and hairy and the closest living cousin of the woolly rhino, is down to a few dozen. The Javan rhino is confined to a single park in Indonesia. The greater one-horned rhino of India and Nepal is the counterexample: reduced to perhaps two hundred animals a century ago, protected hard, and now numbering around four thousand. Which returns us to the fingernail. Rhinos are not vanishing because they are badly designed, or because the climate turned on them. They survived the Ice Age. They are vanishing because a spike of compacted protein, which does nothing that a chewed fingernail could not do, is sold by weight at the price of gold. An order that ruled the planet's grasslands for thirty million years is being dismantled over a misunderstanding about hair.
